# The Botanical Confession

*Book Two of The Blackwood Ridge Mysteries*

Word count: 22,624 — a novella

***

## The Estate Lot

The peonies on the square had come in early that year.

Callie noticed them on the walk down — not from the apartment stairs to the shop front, the short way, but the long way, out the back and around through the square, because she had got into the habit of pretending she needed the morning air when what she needed was to prove the morning would still have her. The peonies were bowing under their own heads in the brick planter by the gazebo, the white ones going brown at the edges because no one on the council had thought to deadhead them. Late May. The light had a pressed-glass quality it got in the valley before summer hardened everything to brass, and the town smelled of wet stone and something sweet and rotting underneath that she chose to call magnolia.

She held her tea in both hands. Bergamot. She had reclaimed it in the weeks since — reclaimed the shop, the back room, the glass, the ritual of the morning cup — and the reclamation had held, more or less, the way a set bone holds. You could walk on it. You did not quite trust it. The tea was almost right. There was a register it hit when she was a girl, Eleanor at the long table, the steam rising between them, that she could not seem to find again, and she had stopped trying to name what was missing and settled for the fact of the warmth in her hands.

Harlan Beech was sweeping the stretch of pavement outside the hardware store, and he did not look up when she passed. He had not looked up in a week. He had always looked up before — tipped his chin, called out something about the weather, asked after the shop. Now the broom moved, and his eyes moved with it, and Callie walked past with her tea and said nothing and received nothing back.

At the far corner, Donna Rives was unlocking the post office, and she did look up — and then she did not, her hand going slow on the key as if she'd forgotten what she was doing, her face closing like a door pulled gently to. Donna had come to the shop every Thursday for a decade, for the romance paperbacks and the gossip and the half-hour of warmth. She had not come since March. Callie had not counted the Thursdays because counting them would have been admitting she'd noticed, and noticing would have been admitting it hurt, and the whole architecture of the last months had been built on not admitting that.

She walked through the square with the particular care of a woman who has learned that the town is looking at her and not quite meeting her eyes, and that the not-quite has a weight. She had pulled the thread — the Ralston fraud, the murdered minister, the whole buried founding of the town — and the town had come apart a little, and the coming-apart had a taste: a flinching, the way you pull back from a hot stove before you've decided whether it burned you. They did not hate her. They wished she had not made them know what they knew.

She let herself in through the front. The bell rang. The shop exhaled — old leather, bergamot, the faint must of paper that has not been opened in a decade — and for a moment she stood in the doorway with her tea and let the smell do what it did, which was to tell her she was home in a place that was also the place her mother had died, and that these two facts had not yet finished arguing. The reading lamps were off. The front table held yesterday's acquisitions, unpriced. The shop waited the way the book waited — patiently, with the certainty of something that would still be here when she was ready.

The book was on the worktable in the back room where she had left it. She had not moved it. Since December — the night she'd found it, the unremarkable nineteenth-century botanical with margins full of a hand she did not know, small and precise and oddly steady — she had walked past it forty times and not picked up the glass. She knew what curiosity cost.

The book waited. Books did that.

She was standing in the doorway of the back room, her tea going cold, looking at the open page without seeing it, when the bell rang at the front of the shop.

It was Eli.

He came in carrying a crate, the kind the auction house used for paper lots, and he was halfway through a sentence before he was through the door — "I can come back, I can leave it, sorry, I should have called—" and then he caught himself, and stopped, and stood straighter, and said, "Morning, Callie," and she saw, with a small pang she did not examine, that he was practicing being a person who did not apologize for taking up space.

He was getting better at it. There was color in him that had not been there in the winter. He'd cut his hair. He was wearing a shirt with buttons, which was new, and which he kept touching at the collar as if he'd forgotten he'd put it on.

"Morning, Eli."

He set the crate on the counter. "The rest of the Dabney lot. The paperwork finally cleared. I split out the trade paperbacks for the shelf lot but there's a few you'll want to price yourself." He hesitated. "And there's, um. A thing. With the provenance. I thought you'd want to know."

Eli did not usually say things like *provenance*. She looked at him.

"The Dabney estate," he said. "I didn't put it together when the lot first came in, but — you know how Marguerite Dabney died? Last week? The cancer, it was — anyway. The lot's hers. The whole lot. And the botanical, the one you set aside in December, the one with the—" He stopped. Swallowed. Started over, more carefully, as if he'd rehearsed this part. "I was logging the rest of it and I found her initials in three more volumes. Same ink. Same hand. So the botanical's hers. It was always hers. I just — I thought you'd want to know. Whose hand it was."

Callie set her tea down.

She had not known whose hand it was. She had, in fact, made a kind of peace with not knowing — had filed the book under *later*, under *when the town has forgiven you enough to afford a new curiosity*, which was a filing system that had the advantage of never requiring her to open the drawer. And now Eli Townsend, who six months ago had hidden in the back of the auction house and apologized for breathing, had opened the drawer for her.

Marguerite Dabney. The English teacher, the garden-club woman — sharp, exact, respected more than she was warmed to. Callie had spoken to her perhaps four times. The last time, on the square, Marguerite had looked at her and said, "You read what other people leave in the margins, don't you." Not a question. A naming. Callie had said something deflecting, and Marguerite had smiled — the corners of her mouth going one way and her eyes going another — and said, "Good. That's a rare thing," and then she'd gathered her bag and gone, and Callie had not thought about it again except for the small uncomfortable heat of being seen precisely by a woman she had not given permission to see her.

Dead. Of cancer. Last week.

And the hand on the botanical was hers.

"Eli," she said. "Thank you."

He flushed. "I didn't do anything. I just — you always say the provenance is the thing. So." He touched his collar again. Then, more quietly: "How did you know? That it mattered? The book. When you set it aside in December. How did you know to look?"

She should have said something professional. *The ink was modern, the hand was deliberate, the annotations were systematic.* All true. None of it was the answer.

"The ink's modern, the hand is systematic," she said — the professional answer, the safe one. She stopped. Tried again. "A hand that careful isn't decorating. It wants to be read. Most people don't look closely enough to see the difference."

She heard Eleanor in it as she said it. She heard it and let it go.

Eli nodded, slowly. Then he said, "I'll get the rest of the crate," and went back out to the van, and Callie was alone with the book.

She did not pick up the glass. Not yet.

She went to the counter instead. She pulled a pricing guide from the shelf and opened it and began listing the trade paperbacks Eli had left — mysteries, romance, a few westerns, the kind of clean stock that moved on the front table. She wrote the prices in pencil on the inside flaps the way she had done ten thousand times, the way Eleanor had taught her, the way the shop had always run. The work was ordinary and it was what she had, and she did it for twenty minutes, and she did not think about the book, and the not-thinking was its own kind of thinking, and the pencil moved and the prices stacked up and the morning came through the window in long gold bars across the floor, and then she was at the back room doorway again, and she did not remember standing up from the counter.

She stood at the worktable and she looked at the open page, and she let herself, for the first time since December, really look. The plate was a violet — *Viola odorata*, the sweet violet, hand-colored in a wash that had gone the color of a bruise over a century. And in the margin, in that small steady blue-black hand, Marguerite Dabney had written a name. Lauren. And a date. June 1994. And beneath the date, in the not-quite-English shorthand that Callie had not been able to crack in December and could not crack now, a line of compressed text — fragments of a word, a place, something she almost recognized but couldn't hold.

Callie picked up the glass.

The brass was warm from the table. Her mother's glass — no, hers now, hers by choice and not by ghost, she had earned that much in the winter even if she had not earned much else. She held it over the margin and she felt it begin, the thing she had no better word for than the narrowing: the room drawing down, the world contracting to the circle of light under the lens, to ink and intention and the ghost of the hand that had made it. The paper under the glass took on a texture the naked eye couldn't catch — the faint ridging of the plate's hand-coloring, the way the pigment had settled into the paper's grain over a century, the microscopic foxing at the edges like a bruise working inward. And in the margin, magnified, the ink lived. She could see the hairline stroke where the pen had first touched the page, the slight pool of blue-black at the foot of each *L* where Marguerite had paused — barely, the way a teacher pauses between thoughts — before setting the next letter down. She could feel the hand now that she knew whose it was. Not the fear that had been in Jacob Wren's cramped cipher, not Pike's eager downhill slant, not Eleanor's looping familiar voice. This was a steady hand. A patient hand. The hand of a woman who had sat down with this book and gone through it page by page and written as if she had all the time in the world, and as if she expected, eventually, to be found.

She turned back to the first plate.

A rosemary — *Rosmarinus officinalis* — and in the margin, in the same small steady hand, a single word: *remembrance*. Not the Latin, not the common name. The meaning. Marguerite had annotated each plate with the flower's language, the old Victorian game the garden-club women still played: rosemary for remembrance, and beneath it a date, and a name Callie did not recognize. The next plate was rue — *sorrow, regret* — and beneath it another date, and a phrase in the compressed shorthand. The next was aconite, and aconite meant *hatred*, and Marguerite had written the word out and underlined it once, firmly, as if she had begun to name the hatred and then thought better of letting it show. Then a violet — *faithfulness* — and the name Lauren again, and the same date, and beside it a single letter, an initial: *W.*

The flowers were a key. Callie could feel it the way she felt a hand's character — not yet decoded, but decoding, the structure of it pressing up under the surface like a watermark holding in the sheet. Each plate carried a meaning and a date and a fragment, and together they were not decoration. They were a sentence. A long, careful, patient sentence that a woman had built out of flowers because flowers were the language she trusted, and because the sentence was one she could not bring herself to write in plain words.

She did not crack it that morning. She would not crack it for weeks. But she felt its shape, the way you feel the shape of a room in the dark before you find the light — and the shape was grief, and accusation, and a patience so deliberate it had to be hiding something it could not say any other way.

Callie turned to the final plates.

And there, in the last three, the pen pressure changed.

It was slight. You would not have seen it without the glass. But under the brass the strokes grew lighter, the letters thinner where the hand had been surer before, and in the very last passage the lines crowded together as if the woman writing had run out of room and out of time at once. The ink was the same. The hand was the same. The steadiness was not. Something had changed between the first plate and the last, and Callie understood it: the woman had been dying when she wrote this, and she had known it, and she had written faster. And Callie felt it — the thing Marguerite must have felt, the clock running, the hand that had been patient for thirty years suddenly out of patience, out of time, the letters crowding forward as if the woman could push the meaning onto the page faster if she only pressed hard enough and crowded close enough and did not stop to breathe. Callie had seen hands like this before — in wills, in confessions, in the last pages of diaries where the writer knew the door was closing. The hand was always the same: it knew. And it ran.

She set the glass down. Gently. On the felt rest. She did not let go of it.

In the front of the shop, Eli was shelving the trade paperbacks from the crate, and she could hear him humming — badly, tunelessly, the humming of a young man who had stopped apologizing for the sound of himself. Through the front window the peonies were bowing on the square, going brown at the edges because no one had thought to tend them. Somewhere a dog was barking. The light was still pressed-glass, still sweet, still early.

And under the grey mornings, Callie felt it again — curiosity, the small clean thing — and with it a second thing she would not name: the knowledge that it was going to cost her, and that the choice had already been made the moment she picked up the glass.

Marguerite Dabney had written *Lauren* and *June 1994*, and then she had died, and she had left the book to be found.

Callie picked up her tea. It had gone cold. She drank it anyway.

***

## Floriography

It was planted by meaning.

Callie had walked the three blocks from the square with Marguerite's book under her arm, and the book was heavier than it had been yesterday — heavier with the weight she had agreed to carry when she picked up the glass. She had chosen this. She was paying for it. And now she stood at the gate of the Dabney house, a low Victorian cottage on Pippin Street behind a hedge of boxwood let go just enough to look tended rather than trimmed, and she understood that the garden was the other half of what she had been reading.

Not by color, not by height, not by season — the way every other garden on the street was planted, the way the council planted the square. Marguerite had laid her beds in the old language, the language of flowers, and she had done it with the same patient deliberation she had brought to the margins of the botanical. A rosemary hedge along the front path — *remembrance*, the first word, the same word Callie had read under the glass. Beyond it, a stand of rue bending under the late-spring rain — *sorrow, regret*. A patch of white violets at the corner — *modesty*, a cousin to the sweet violet in the book that meant *faithfulness*, and Callie registered the distinction the way she registered two hands by the same scribe: related, not identical, each carrying its own assignment. And at the center of the back bed, where the light fell cleanest, a single peony in early bloom, and peony in the old language meant *shame*. A whole bed of shame, ringed with rosemary. A woman had lived inside this garden for thirty years and she had planted it as a confession no one but another reader would catch.

The gate was unlatched but not open. She pushed it. It did not creak. It had been oiled recently, and the path beyond was swept, and in the back bed a woman was on her knees with a trowel, turning the soil around the rue.

She was seventy or near it. Narrow, upright, the kind of thin that came from a life of not quite eating enough. Her hair was steel-grey, cut short and practical, and her hands in the soil were the hands of someone who had been doing this for longer than Callie had been alive. She did not look up when the gate opened. She finished the turn she was making, set the trowel down precisely on a folded cloth beside a knitting bag — wool the color of dust, needles crossed in the half-finished scarf trailing from it — and then she stood, slowly, careful of her knees, and she looked at Callie.

"You're the book woman," she said.

It was not a question. Her voice was Virginia, unhurried, the words coming out short and dry and spaced, as if she rationed them.

"Callie Thorne," Callie said. "I — yes."

"She'd have liked that you came." The woman did not offer her name. She did not offer her hand. She picked up the folded cloth, shook the soil from it, folded it again, and set it back over the arm of the garden bench. "She wrote you down for the books. The lawyer brought the list over. Foxed Page, three boxes, the annotated one to be priced by you personally. I thought you'd be by yesterday."

There was nothing to say to that except sorry, and sorry was not the right word, and the woman's face was the kind that did not want the wrong word, so Callie said nothing, and the silence sat between them, and the woman let it sit, and Callie understood that the silence was a test and that she had passed a small corner of it by not filling it.

"You can walk it," the woman said, after a while. "The garden. She'd have liked that too. Don't pull anything up." She turned back to her trowel.

Callie walked the garden.

She walked it slowly, the way she walked a difficult page, and she read it as she went, and the reading was worse than the book had been, because the book had been abstract — a cipher, a puzzle, a hand — and the garden was a life. Here was a bed of rosemary and myrtle — *remembrance* and *love* — and at its head a small stone Marguerite had set the year Lauren went, not a grave — there was no grave — but a place to put the date, chiseled rough: 1994. Here was a patch of narcissus gone late and leggy — *self-love*, or *the return of affection* — and here, against the kitchen wall where the rain came off the eaves, a row of maidenhair fern, and fern in the old language meant *sincerity* and also *secret* and also *magic*, and Marguerite had planted it beneath the window where she must have washed her dishes for thirty years. Through the kitchen window Callie could see a mantel, and on the mantel a photograph in a frame — a girl, seventeen, cap and gown, the smile of someone about to leave. The photo was turned to face the room.

And then she found the bed that had no flower left in it.

It was a square of turned earth at the back, against the fence, where the light did not reach. The soil had been worked recently — you could see the trowel marks — but nothing grew in it. The markers were still there, small wooden stakes with names inked in the same steady hand: *hollyhock*, *yellow rose*, *columbine*. Ambition. Betrayal. Folly. A bed of the qualities Marguerite had wanted to name and had pulled up by the root, leaving only the stakes, only the accusation. She had weeded her own garden of its hatreds, or tried to. The turned earth smelled of iron and rain, and somewhere in the vocabulary a letter surfaced — the *W.* beside Lauren's name on the violet plate — and Callie wondered, with a small cold pull, who the pulled-up flowers had been for. Who Marguerite had accused in a garden no one read.

The peony bed was at the center. *Shame*. Ringed with rosemary — *remembrance*. And between the shame and the remembrance, a single plant Callie had to bend to identify: basil, its leaves small and sharp-scented, bruised green when she brushed them with her fingertips. Basil meant *hatred*, and also *poverty*, and Marguerite had planted it alone and hemmed in by the two heavier meanings, the way a woman contains a thing she has decided to say only to herself. The same word the book's aconite carried — *hatred* — and Callie felt the click of it, the two ciphers locking together: the garden's vocabulary was the cipher's vocabulary. She held the legend now. The book and the ground were one text, and Marguerite had written them both for the same reader.

Callie straightened. The sun had come out from behind the clouds, and the warmth of it landed on the stone path and on Callie's shoulders, and for a moment the garden was just a garden — green, wet, blooming, smelling of earth and rosemary and the sweet decay of late spring — and somewhere inside the cottage a kettle was on, and the smell of plain black tea drifted through the kitchen window, and the woman in the bed was just a woman tending flowers in the morning. Then the woman looked up, and the looking changed it back.

"You read it," the woman said. Not a question. A naming.

"Some of it."

"Marguerite said once there were two kinds of people in this town. The ones who looked at her garden and saw flowers, and the ones who looked at her garden and saw a woman talking to herself." She pulled a weed, examined it, set it aside for the pile. "She preferred the first kind. They left her alone."

The gate clicked behind Callie, and she turned, and it was Mae. And before she saw Mae's face she smelled her — lavender, the sachet-and-cinnamon smell that was Mae's armor, the smell of the kitchen and the parlor and every room Mae had ever filled with warmth so no one asked what she was hiding. The smell was thinner now. Strained. Like everything else about Mae.

Mae stood on the path with a covered dish in her hands and a look on her face that Callie recognized — the warm face, the open face, the face that had come through her shop door a hundred times without knocking — except that now Mae was at the gate and not through it, and her hand was still on the latch, and she had not come in. She was waiting. She was asking to come in.

"Morning, Callie, honey," Mae said. The endearment landed carefully, the way Mae placed things — at once a welcome and a wall. "I brought the casserole for Doris. I didn't know you'd be here."

Doris. The name landed. Callie looked at the woman in the garden bed, the narrow upright woman with the steel-grey hair and the rationed words, and understood: the woman tending the remembrance bed was the woman the remembrance was for.

"Doris Coalter," the woman said, and this time she did offer her name, as if Callie had earned it by standing quiet. She did not say *Lauren was my daughter*. She did not have to. The garden had said it, and the date on the stone had said it, and the careful way Doris Coalter turned back to her trowel said it.

Mae let herself in. She set the casserole on the bench. She stood between them, and her hands worked the dish cloth when she was holding something back. She had been holding something back for months. It had become a posture.

"She asked after you," Mae said, to Doris. "Yesterday. At the Society."

"Marguerite was asking after everyone by the end," Doris said. "She was a woman who liked to know who was coming to her funeral."

"She meant the books, Doris. She wanted to know Callie had them."

Doris's trowel stopped. She did not look up. "She wanted a lot of things, by the end. She didn't always say what they were."

The silence that came after was not the testing silence Doris had given Callie. It was older. It had been standing between these two women for decades, and the garden said it now so they did not have to.

Callie cleared her throat. "The girl," she said. "The date on the stone. 1994."

Doris's hands went flat on her knees. Palms down. Holding herself in place.

"That's not mine to give you," Doris said. "Not today."

"I'm not asking for it."

"You're asking for it by standing in the bed."

Callie looked down. She had, without noticing, stepped off the path and onto the soil of the remembrance bed, and her shoe had pressed a print into the turned earth beside the rosemary. She stepped back.

"I'm sorry."

Doris said nothing. Mae's hands had stopped moving on the cloth. The garden was very quiet, and somewhere over the rooftops a mockingbird was running through every song it had ever stolen, and the light was still sweet and still early and Callie was standing in a dead woman's confession with the dead woman's book under her arm, and the woman who owned the confession's other half was on her knees and would not look at her.

Then Doris said, "Lauren," and the word came out flat, but underneath it something that had been held for thirty-two years was letting the smallest edge show. She pulled a weed. Set it aside. "Lauren Coalter. My daughter. She was seventeen the summer she went. There was a party at the lake." She pulled another weed. "She didn't come home."

A pause. The trowel turned the soil.

"They said she run. She did not run." Doris's voice did not rise. It went flatter, and the flatness was the loudest thing in the garden. "They dragged the lake. They did not find her. They wrote it down 'runaway' and they closed the file and they let me stand at this gate for thirty-two years waiting for a girl who was never coming back down that road."

Her hands stayed flat on her knees, palms down. That was the thing that held Callie's throat — not the words, not the flat voice, the hands. The posture of a woman pressing herself to the earth.

Callie wanted to say something. That she was sorry. That it should not have taken thirty-two years. That the woman lying in the bed she was kneeling in had tried, at the end, to make up for all the years she had not tried. But all of it was the wrong word, and Doris's face was the face that did not want the wrong word, and so Callie stood in the turned earth of the remembrance bed and said nothing.

Mae made a small sound. Not a word. The sound of a woman who had heard the shape of this before — and Callie understood, looking between them, that Mae recognized it. Not the specifics. The shape. A woman carrying a silence she'd decided the town couldn't afford. The way Mae had carried hers about the Ralstons, and had done with it what she had done: kept it, out of love, out of cost.

"You think she wrote it down," Doris said. She was looking at Callie now, really looking, and underneath the flatness something had come loose. "Marguerite. In the book. You think she wrote down what happened to my girl."

"I think she tried," Callie said.

"Then you find it." Doris's voice did not rise. "You find it, and you bring it to me, and you do not bring it to anyone else first. Not the sheriff. Not the town. Me. She was mine. Whatever's in that book is mine. You understand."

"I understand."

Doris turned back to her trowel. The interview was over.

Mae walked Callie to the gate. She did not touch her. At the gate she stopped, and her hand went to the latch, and she opened it and held it, and for a moment the two of them stood in the small ordinariness of a gate being held. Mae had come. Mae had stood between them. Mae had not begged her to stop the way she had begged her about the Ralstons, and the absence of the begging was its own sentence — the sentence of a woman who had watched one truth tear the town and could not bring herself to ask for another, and who would not forgive Callie for not needing to be asked.

"You'll do it anyway," Mae said. Quietly. Not a question. Her thumb worked the latch. "Lord, Callie."

"Yes."

Mae nodded. She did not say *be careful*. She did not say *I'm sorry*. She let go of the gate and turned back toward the cottage, toward the casserole and the woman who would not leave her alone in her grief, and Callie walked out onto Pippin Street with the book under her arm and the smell of rosemary on her hands where she had brushed the hedge.

The rosemary meant remembrance, and the remembrance meant thirty-two years, and thirty-two years was a long time for a woman to kneel in a bed she had planted as a confession and wait for someone to read it.

Callie walked home the long way, through the square, and the peonies were still bowing, and the town still did not quite meet her eyes, and under her arm Marguerite's book had grown heavier, because it was not a puzzle anymore. It was a girl. A girl who had not come home. And the book was the other half of what the garden had said — the half that could travel, the half Marguerite had aimed at her — and she had not cracked it yet, and she would, and the cracking would cost her, and the cost was the point.

***

## The Open Palm

She worked on the book for two days, and the worst of it was that she liked it.

The shop still had to run — the morning customers who still came, the small stubborn core of them who had not stopped meeting her eyes, the mail, the cataloguing of the rest of the Dabney lot, which Eli had left in a neat stack by the counter with a note in his careful new handwriting, *thought you'd want to price these yourself — E*. But in the back room, between the commerce, with the glass and the lamp and the pot of bergamot going cold at her elbow, she worked. And the work was a pleasure, and the pleasure was the danger of it, because Doris Coalter's voice was still in her ear — *you find it, and you bring it to me, and you do not bring it to anyone else first* — and the finding was the part that had always let Callie stop thinking about the rest.

The flowers were the key.

Each plate carried its Victorian meaning, written out in the margin in Marguerite's small steady hand, and the meanings were not decoration. They were a vocabulary. *Rosemary*, *remembrance*. *Rue*, *regret*. *Yarrow*, *war*. *Basil*, *hatred*. *Violet*, *faithfulness* — and here Marguerite had written *Lauren* again, and the date, and the initial *W.* Read in sequence, the flowers spelled something. Not a sentence, exactly. A ledger.

The harder layer was the shorthand.

The wider margins held passages in a script that was not quite English and not quite anything Callie could name — compressed, abbreviated, the words run together and the vowels dropped, ten thousand graded papers worth of private telegraph. Callie had seen shorthand like it once, in a Victorian governess's diary that had come through the shop, and once in her own mother's end-of-term notes, which Eleanor had kept in a kind of private code that Callie had learned to read as a girl because reading it had felt like being let into a room. Marguerite's shorthand was its own animal, but it was kin to those, and by the second afternoon Callie was cracking it the way you crack a lock — a little at a time, the tumblers turning, the meaning catching and then giving and then catching again.

She had, by Tuesday evening, a skeleton.

June 1994. A party. The lake. *Lauren* — faithful, the violet said. *Ambler* — a name, written beside a plate of yarrow, and yarrow meant *war*, and also it meant *cure*, and Marguerite had written the name and underlined it once, very cleanly, and gone on. And beside the date, in the shorthand she had not yet cracked, a single word she could make out: *dock*. The rest of the phrase was pressed into almost nothing — the vowels gone, the consonants run together — and the not-knowing of it sat in her throat.

Marguerite had marked something. At a dock. In June 1994. Something to do with a girl named Lauren and a name written beside war.

She needed context. She needed to know who Lauren had been to the town, and who Ambler was, and what the lake had meant that summer. And there was exactly one place in Blackwood Ridge that held the shape of a girl who had been seventeen in 1994, and that was the school.

She went on Wednesday morning.

Blackwood Ridge High sat on the east edge of town, a brick building from the sixties built over an older foundation, the kind of school where the trophy case went back decades and the photographs in the front hall yellowed in their frames until the faces turned the color of weak tea. Callie had not been inside it since she herself had been a student, and the smell of it hit her at the door — floor wax, pencil shavings, the particular stale-sweet air of a building full of children — and for an instant she was seventeen again, and she hated the instant, and she walked through it.

The principal's office was at the end of the front hall. The door was open. The name on the frosted glass said *W. Ambler, Principal*. Ambler. The name from the margin, underlined once beside the plate of yarrow. She had come looking for context on a girl who had been seventeen in 1994, and the school had put the name off the page onto the glass.

She knocked on the open door.

He was behind a desk piled with paper, a tall man in a pressed shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow, greying at the temples — she'd heard two women on the square say so, in a voice that wasn't quite about his temples. He was reading a letter and frowning at it, and when he looked up the frown turned, smoothly, into a smile, and the smile was warm. It was genuinely warm. She registered that first. Warmth could be a perimeter.

"Callie Thorne," he said. He stood. He came around the desk with his hand out. "I was hoping you'd come by. I heard you had the Dabney books. Marguerite spoke of you often."

His hand was open. Palm shown, fingers relaxed, the gesture of a man who had nothing to hide. She took it, and the grip was firm and dry and exactly the right length, and when he let go his hand went back to his side, open, the palm still displayed for a beat before it turned naturally away. She filed it the way she filed a hand's character — under *deliberate*, under *practiced* — and let it go. One handshake was not evidence.

"Mr. Ambler," she said.

"Wells," he said. "Everyone calls me Wells. Sit, sit. I've got the kettle on — the staff room is a crime scene, don't drink that, but I keep a decent cup in here. Tea? Coffee?"

"Tea. Thank you."

He made it. He moved around the small office with the ease of a man who had made ten thousand cups of tea for ten thousand uncomfortable conversations, easy, anecdotal, his voice doing the work it knew how to do. He asked about the shop. He asked about Eleanor — gently, with the practiced care of a man who knows which deaths are recent enough to hurt. He asked how the town was treating her, and his eyes did a thing when he asked it, a small flicker, the faintest register of *and I know it hasn't been easy*, and then the warmth came back and covered it. Wells Ambler listened for the weather in a room and adjusted his own temperature to match it. It was a real gift. It was also, she thought, a way of never quite being caught in any single weather of his own.

"You knew Marguerite," she said, when the tea was poured and they were seated.

"I did." He set his cup down. His hand, on the desk, was open, the fingers spread, the gesture of a man spreading his cards. "She was my teacher, a long time ago. Then my colleague. Then — well, then the kind of older woman who tells you when you've got it wrong and means it as a kindness. I'll miss her. The whole town will."

"She taught you," Callie said. It was not a question. She was placing him. If he had been Marguerite's student, he had been in Blackwood Ridge in the early nineties. If he had been in Blackwood Ridge in the early nineties, he had been here the summer Lauren Coalter vanished.

"English," he said. "Junior year. She made us read everything twice. She said the first reading was for the plot and the second was for the truth." He smiled. The smile was sad, and real, and it was the sadness of a man remembering a woman who had mattered to him. "She was right, of course. She usually was."

He told a story then, about Marguerite failing him on a paper he'd been proud of — junior year, *The Great Gatsby*, he'd written ten pages on the green light and she'd handed it back with a single word in the margin: *again* — and he told it well, with timing, with the self-deprecating warmth of a man who has learned that the best way to make a room comfortable is to offer himself as the joke. And Callie laughed. She did not want to laugh, because she had come in wary and she wanted to stay wary, but he was funny, and the story was kind, and the kindness was real. She liked him. That was the thing to watch — liking was what made you stop looking, and she had come here to look.

"And Lauren Coalter," Callie said.

The office went very quiet.

It was a small thing. It was the smallest thing. The smile did not leave his face — it stayed exactly where it was, in exactly the shape it had been — but for one beat it became a thing that was being held rather than a thing that was happening, and his open hand on the desk did not move, and then it did move, very slowly, to close around his cup, and the closing was the first time she had seen his hand not be open.

"Lauren," he said. He looked down at his cup. He looked up. "Where did that name come from, Callie?"

"In the book," she said. "In the margins. Marguerite wrote it more than once."

He was quiet for a moment. Then he nodded, slowly, as if he had been expecting something like this and was sorry to have been right.

"Lauren was my girlfriend," he said. "The summer we graduated. She was — she was bright. She was going to get out of here. She had a plan." His voice had thinned. Not cracked — thinned. The warmth was still there, but it was stretched over something, the way a sheet of ice stretches over moving water. "She went to a party at the lake that June. She never came home. They said she ran. I've never believed it. I've never not believed it. You live with a thing like that for thirty-two years and you stop knowing what you believe. You just know she's gone."

"I'm sorry," Callie said.

"Everyone's sorry." He said it without bitterness. He said it the way Doris had said things — flat, dry, rationed — and then the warmth came back, and he smiled, and the smile was the sad one again. "Can I tell you something, Callie? I've spent my whole life trying to be the kind of man she would have wanted. The kind of man worth her. I became a teacher because of Marguerite. I came back here because of Lauren. Everything good I've done, I've done because of a girl who didn't come home. That's not — it's not a confession. It's just the shape of it. You understand."

She understood that he was telling her the truth. She also understood that the truth he was telling her was the shape he had decided on thirty-two years ago and polished until it was the only shape left.

"Is there anything you remember," she said, carefully, "about that night? Anything Marguerite might have — anything that stuck."

His hand closed on the cup again. The open palm was gone. When he answered, his voice was steady and warm and a half-degree cooler than it had been.

"I was at the party," he said. "I saw her early in the evening. We argued. I went home. I didn't see her again." He spread his hands — open, palms up, the gesture of a man showing he has nothing. "That's all I have. That's all I've ever had."

"Did anyone see you leave?"

The palms stayed up. They stayed up a beat too long.

"Callie." He said her name the way he said everything — gently, like a kindness. "I was nineteen and heartsick and I went home and put myself to bed, and I have spent thirty-two years wishing I had stayed at that party. That is the whole of what I have. I don't know what you are looking for in those margins, but I don't think it's in this office." He stood. The gesture was warm. It was also, very cleanly, the end of the interview. "You're welcome back any time. The kettle's always on."

She thanked him for the tea. She let him show her out, and on the walk back to the shop the open palm stayed in her mind like a mark on a page. She did not know yet what it marked. Only that it was deliberate.

The sheriff was waiting at the shop.

He was leaning against the hood of his cruiser in the way he had, arms crossed, hat on, taking up the whole of the pavement in front of The Foxed Page, and when she came around the corner he did not uncross his arms, and he did not take off his hat, and the not-doing of those things was its own sentence.

"Callie," he said.

"Sheriff."

"I hear you've been asking after Marguerite Dabney's books."

"I bought the lot. It's my job to ask after them."

He rubbed the back of his neck. She had seen him do it a hundred times. It was what he did when he was out of his depth and did not want anyone to know.

"Marguerite Dabney died of cancer," he said. "Last week. In her bed. There is no crime here, Callie. There is a woman who died naturally, and a book full of old notes, and a girl who ran away in 1994, and a town that just spent the winter coming apart at the seams over a different dead man and does not need you pulling at this one. You understand what I'm saying."

"I understand what you're saying."

"Then leave it alone."

"Wells Ambler was her student," Callie said. "He was at the party."

The sheriff's jaw set. That was the tell — not the neck, the jaw. He had not expected the name.

"Wells is a friend of mine," he said. Quiet. Final. "He sat with me through the winter, when half this town wouldn't speak to either of us. I am not going to pull him into a thing like this on the strength of a dead woman's flowers. I won't do it, Callie."

She looked at him. He was not a stupid man. He was a man whose definition of evidence had walls, and everything outside the walls was weather, and weather was not his department. She had liked that about him, once. She had needed that about him, once, the winter before, when his walls had almost let the wrong man hang. And now the walls were doing something else — they were sheltering a man he sat with, a man he owed — and the sheltering looked the same as the blindness, and maybe was the same, and that was the thing she could not say to him.

"There's a name in the margins," she said. "A date. A place by water. It may be nothing. It may be Marguerite remembering something she couldn't prove. I won't know until I've read the rest." She set her hand on the shop door; the steadiness cost her something, and she let it cost.

"And when you've read the rest."

"Then I'll bring it to you."

He rubbed his neck again. He put his hat straight. He got in the cruiser without another word, and she stood on the pavement and watched him go, and the open palm and the word *dock* turned over in her mind, and she knew, standing there in the late-spring light with the bergamot still on her tongue from Wells Ambler's kettle, that she had begun, very quietly, to look sideways at a man the whole town loved.

She went inside. She picked up the glass. She turned to the next plate, and the flower was yarrow, and yarrow meant *war*, and beside it, in Marguerite's hand, was the name Ambler, and the date, and the word *dock*, and the rest of the shorthand — the part Marguerite had crushed almost to nothing — would not give. She worked it the rest of the afternoon. The tumbler would not turn.

That was all right. She had not expected it to be quick.

The bergamot was still on her tongue. The open palm would not leave her. *Deliberate* — a word she had learned, the winter before, to trust.

She had begun to look sideways at a man the whole town loved, and she knew what that cost. She had watched Gus Ralston's name leave the mouth of every person in Blackwood Ridge who had ever said it kindly, and she had watched the town learn the shape of its own founding lie, and she had not been forgiven for either. She would not be forgiven for this.

She sat in the lamp's gold light with the undecoded shorthand and the word *dock*. She was going to cross the distance between what she had and what she needed. She knew what it would cost. She had already decided to pay it.

***

## The Wet Hemline

The plate was meadowsweet.

*Filipendula ulmaria* — hand-colored in a greenish wash gone the color of pond water over a century, the tiny clustered flowers drawn with the stiff precision of a Victorian engraver who had never seen the plant in the wild and was working from a pressed specimen. In the old language meadowsweet meant *uselessness*, and also it meant *the stifling of a feeling*, and Marguerite had written both meanings in the margin, one above the other, and underlined the second.

Callie worked the shorthand beneath it. The dock passage from the yarrow plate still resisted — compressed to almost nothing — but the meadowsweet passage was longer, and it gave.

Four lines compressed into the space of two, the vowels dropped, the consonants run together with the pen pressure of a woman who had held this particular sentence inside her for thirty-two years and could feel it, now, in the last months of her life, trying to get out faster than her hand could fairly take it down. Callie held the glass over it. The brass was warm. The lamp had gone gold. The tea at her elbow had gone cold again, and she did not notice, because the narrowing had taken her — the room drawn down, the world contracted to the greenish wash of the plate, to ink and intention.

The tumbler turned.

*He came up the lake path after dark. I was at the kitchen window. The light was on. He did not see me. He was wet to the knees.*

Callie read it again.

*He was wet to the knees and the legs of his trousers were dark with it and he walked in the middle of the road so as not to step in the dust. I thought he had been swimming. Then I thought he had not been swimming. The way he walked. He came to the Carmody place and he told them he had been at the Harlow barn. I know this because Helen Carmody told me the next week, at the club meeting. He told them he had been at the Harlow barn all evening. He had not been at the Harlow barn. He had been at the lake. He had been at the lake and he was wet to the knees, and he had come back alone, and Lauren had not come home.*

Callie set the glass down.

She sat back in the chair and she looked at the margin the way you look at a face that has just said something you cannot unhear. The back room was very quiet. Through the doorway she could see the front of the shop, the shelves, the reading lamp, the closed sign she had not turned over since morning. The bell had not rung in two hours. Outside, the late-spring light was going long and gold across the square, and somewhere a lawnmower was droning, and the peonies were bowing in their planters, and inside the margins of a nineteenth-century book about flowers a dead woman had written, in her small steady hand, that she had seen a boy come home wet.

Not *he killed her.* Not *he is guilty.* Marguerite had not written those words. She had written what she had seen. A date. A place by water. A name. A wet hemline. And the careful, deliberate, rationed refusal to go one syllable past the seeing.

The wet hemline.

Callie could see it. That was the thing the cipher did that no secondhand account could do — it put the seeing in her own head. The kitchen window. The light on. The boy in the middle of the road, walking to keep the dust off his shoes because his trousers were soaked below the knees. He had been at the lake. He had come back alone. Lauren had not come home. And Marguerite had stood at her window with the light on and she had seen, and she had done the careful thing, which was nothing.

The tea was cold. She drank it anyway. It tasted like nothing in particular, which was its own answer.

She tested it the way she tested every hand — against the counter-narrative. Marguerite had been dying. Cancer in the last months, the pen pressure fading in the final plates. A woman in pain, annotating a book she loved, possibly reading patterns into old memories that were not there. A wet hemline was not a confession. A boy coming home from a lake was not a killing. Marguerite might have been wrong.

The doubt sat where it always sat — behind the certainty, not loud enough to stop the work, but loud enough to keep it honest.

She needed corroboration. The school's records for 1994 — who had been in Marguerite's junior English, who had been at the lake that summer, who had been at the Harlow barn if anyone had. She had been planning to pull them from the county archive on Thursday. She was sitting with the book open, turning the logistics over, when she heard the lock turn at the front.

It was after five. She had not opened the shop since morning. She stood, and the back of her neck ached from the hours hunched over the glass, and she came through the doorway and found Harriet Vailes at the counter, setting her bag down with the particular care of a woman who has come on an errand she would rather not be running.

Harriet was on the town council. She was also a docent at the school's alumni events, and a woman who had raised four children who had all gone through Blackwood Ridge High. Her hand stayed on the bag strap, the knuckles whitening — the grip of a woman holding herself to a task she would rather walk away from. Until March she had come into The Foxed Page every other Friday for the new acquisitions list.

"Callie," Harriet said. She did not unbend her mouth into a smile. "I won't keep you. I wanted to let you know, before you heard it from the office, that the archive key is being recalled for rekeying. The council voted last week. Something about the lock cylinders — security audit. It may be a few weeks before the new system is in."

Callie looked at her.

"The archive has had the same lock for fourteen years," Callie said.

"Well." Harriet touched her bag. "Things change."

"Harriet."

The woman stopped.

"Wells spoke to me," Harriet said. Quietly. Not meeting Callie's eyes. "He's concerned. He used the word *crusade*. He was kind about it — he said he admired your dedication." She paused. "He said it at the council meeting on Tuesday."

The archive key. The 1994 enrollment records. The corroborating names she had been planning to pull on Thursday — the names that would tell her whether Marguerite had been a careful woman or a dying woman seeing patterns that were not there. Wells Ambler had not come to her door and threatened her. He had gone to the council, and he had spoken kindly, admiringly, and the door had closed.

She felt it then — not the craft of it, not the architecture, but the specific shape of the hurt. He was making her the town's wound again. The woman who pulled threads. The woman the town flinched from on contact. She had been that woman all winter, and she had barely survived it. Not with fists. Not with threats. With the town's own exhausted desire to be left alone. He did not have to silence her. He only had to make the town wish she would silence herself.

"Thank you, Harriet," Callie said.

Harriet left quickly. She did not buy anything. She did not look back.

Callie locked the shop. She went to tell Doris.

She went because she had promised. Doris Coalter had said *you find it, and you bring it to me*, and the cipher had a hemline in it, and Doris deserved to know that the dead woman's book was not decoration. She knew it was the wrong thing — she knew it before she reached the end of Pippin Street, the rosemary smell rising from the hedges as the evening dew released it — but the promise was older than the caution, and she walked.

The Dabney gate was open. The garden was in the last of the light. And at the kitchen door of the cottage, on the step where the rosemary hedge grew thick and fragrant, Wells Ambler was setting down a paper bag of groceries.

He did not see Callie at the gate. He was turned away, speaking through the screen door, and his voice carried in the still evening air, a baritone that had spoken in hallways and auditoriums and kitchens for thirty years and had never had to raise it to be heard.

"—the tomatoes are from the garden, they're early this year, I thought you might — Doris, I can come back. I don't have to stay. I wanted to make sure you'd eat."

Doris's voice came from inside, dry, thin. "You don't have to check on me, Wells."

"I know I don't have to." A pause. The gentleness in it was real. Callie could hear that it was real, and the hearing was the worst part, because the man who had come back wet from a lake in 1994 was standing on the step of the mother of the girl who had not come home, and he was bringing her tomatoes from his garden, and he had built this so carefully over the grave that he could no longer find the seam.

"You should eat," Wells said.

Doris said nothing for a moment. Then the screen door opened wider, and Callie saw, through the gap, Doris's hand take the bag, and the hand was steady — the steadiness of a woman who had let this man into her kitchen for thirty years because the kitchen was quiet and he had loved her daughter, or said he had.

Wells came down the path. He saw Callie at the gate.

He stopped.

It was a small stop — a half-beat, a thing measured in fractions of a second — and then he smiled, and the smile came, and it was warm, and it was the smile of a man who has just realized that the room he is in has changed weather.

"Callie," he said. He used her name, easily, remembered, the name of a person he had decided to know. "I didn't know you and Doris were acquainted."

"We met through Marguerite's garden."

"Of course." He nodded. He came to the gate and he stood there, and his hand went to the latch, and the hand was open. Palm shown. The gesture she had filed under *deliberate* two days ago. "How's the decoding coming? I've been thinking about what you said — about the margins. Marguerite was such a careful woman."

He was testing. She could feel it the way she felt a hand's character — in the pen pressure, in the rhythm, in the thing underneath the rhythm that the rhythm was trying to cover. He was testing what she knew, and he was doing it with warmth, and the warmth was thinner than it had been in his office, the way ice thins over moving water.

"It's coming," Callie said. "She was careful. You're right."

His smile held. His eyes did not. Something behind them had gone to attention — a stillness that the rest of his body was working hard to keep easy. "If I can help. You know where to find me."

"I do."

He let go of the gate. He walked past her, and as he passed he put a hand on the gatepost — briefly, lightly — and she saw his hand on the wood, and the hand was open, and the open palm was no longer the gesture of a man who has nothing to hide. It was the gesture of a man who has practiced having nothing to hide for so long that the practice has become the hiding, and she knew, and he did not know she knew, and the knowing sat between them on the path like a stone neither of them was going to pick up.

He went down Pippin Street. He did not look back.

Callie went up the path to the kitchen door. The screen was still open. Doris was at the table, and the grocery bag was in front of her, and she was not unpacking it. She was sitting with her hands in her lap, and the knitting was on the table beside the bag, the half-finished scarf with its needles crossed, and Doris was not knitting. She was looking at the bag.

"Doris," Callie said from the door.

Doris did not look up for a moment. When she did, her face was the face Callie had seen in the garden — dry, watchful, rationed — but the hands in her lap had gone flat, palms down on her thighs, the posture of a woman holding herself in place.

"You saw him," Doris said.

"I saw him."

"He brings me groceries." Doris said it flat. "He's brought me groceries every Thursday for thirty years. He sat in that chair when my husband died. He walked Lauren to the bus stop in the mornings because she'd sleep through her alarm. He's the only one who came."

"I know."

Doris looked at her, and the understanding moved across her face like weather.

"You think it's him," Doris said. "In the book. You think Marguerite wrote down that it was him."

"I think she wrote down what she saw," Callie said carefully. "Not that he did it. She wouldn't write that. She wrote what she —"

"I told you to bring it to me." Doris's voice did not rise. It went flatter, and shorter, and the shortness was a door closing. "I told you. Not him. Me."

"I haven't told anyone, Doris."

"You're standing in his kitchen." Doris's hands pressed flatter on her thighs. "This is his kitchen. He built this kitchen. He put the floor in when the boards rotted. He fixed the window when it wouldn't stay up. You think I don't know what you're telling me? You're telling me the man who put my floor in killed my girl."

"I'm telling you a woman saw him come home wet from a lake the night Lauren didn't come home. That's what she wrote. That's all she wrote."

"That's not all." Doris's jaw set. She went white along the cheekbones, the white of a woman who has been steady for thirty-two years and feels, for the first time, the steadiness costing her something. "You bring me proof, Callie. Not a wet hemline from thirty years ago. The man brought me tomatoes today. He's the only person who — "

She stopped.

The kitchen was very quiet. The grocery bag sat between them on the table, and inside it were tomatoes from Wells Ambler's garden, and they were early that year, and they were real, and the bag was the whole knot of it — penance and cover and cruelty and care — and Doris could not give it up on the strength of a margin note in a dead woman's hand, and Callie knew she could not.

"I'm sorry," Callie said.

"You find the rest," Doris said. Her voice was flat and final. "You find the rest of it before you come to my kitchen again." Her hands came off her thighs and went to the scarf and picked up the needles, and the needles were shaking, and Doris Coalter, who had not shaken in thirty-two years, was shaking now, and she put the needles down again because she could not make them work.

Callie left. She closed the screen door behind her, gently, the way you close a door on a room where someone is sitting with something they cannot yet survive. The rosemary smell rose around her, thick and sweet, and it meant *remembrance*, and remembrance was the only thing Marguerite had ever asked for, and it was the cruelest thing in the garden.

She walked home through the square. The light had gone. The peonies were dark shapes in their planters. Harlan Beech's storefront was shuttered. The town was settling into its evening, the windows going yellow, the sounds of supper behind screen doors. She thought of Doris, sitting with the bag she could not unpack. She thought of Wells, going home to his wife and his children, steady and kind. She could not make the two things fit together, and she did not try.

Callie let herself into the shop. She did not turn on the lights. She went to the back room and sat at the table with the book under the lamp. The meadowsweet plate — *the stifling of a feeling* — and the margin where Marguerite had written, in her small steady hand, *he was wet to the knees*.

She sat with it. The town had closed the archive. Doris had closed her kitchen. The only ally she had was a dead woman who had chosen, thirty years too late, to write down what she had seen and not one word more.

She picked up her tea. It had gone cold hours ago. She drank it. Almost right. Not quite. And she turned to the next plate, because there was nothing else to do, and Marguerite had left her more.

***

## The Language of Flowers

She cracked it on a Thursday.

Not all at once — the cipher had been giving in stages for days, each plate yielding its layer the way a pressed flower gives its color when you moisten it, slowly, the pigment blooming back into the leaf. But Thursday was the day the last tumbler turned, and the whole lock opened, and Callie sat back in the chair with the lamp gold and the tea cold and the shop closed and the archive key still not returned and Doris's kitchen still shut to her, and the book lay open across the table like a body on a slab, and she saw what Marguerite Dabney had done.

It was a map.

Not a confession. Not an accusation. A map. Each plate was a coordinate — the dates clicking into a timeline, the names into a cast, the seeing into evidence. The rosemary gave *remembrance* and the date. The violet gave *faithfulness* and the name. The yarrow gave *war* and the second name, the one underlined once and left. The meadowsweet gave the seeing. And the last plates, the ones where the pen pressure lightened and the letters thinned, gave the place.

The flower was water lily. *Nymphaea alba* — hand-colored in a blue-green wash, the petals drawn half-open, the kind of plate that existed to be beautiful and Marguerite had repurposed it to be precise. Water lily in the old language meant *purity of heart*, and also it meant *the surface and what is under it*, and Marguerite had written the second meaning and underlined it.

Callie held the glass over the shorthand beneath it. Four words, compressed to almost nothing — the vowels crushed, the consonants welded together, the hand of a woman running out of time and out of strength. The brass was warm. The lamp threw gold across the page. She worked it letter by letter — the pen pressure first, then the rhythm, then the ghost of the intention under the rhythm. Twenty minutes. The last of the afternoon light.

*The old dock. The deep.*

The map assembled in her mind — Cedar Lake. Blackwater Cove. The old dock that had been gone for years, the deep silted cove where the water was dark and cold and the town had stopped swimming a decade after Lauren Coalter vanished because the place felt wrong in a way no one had ever named.

Marguerite had named it.

Not *he killed her.* The cipher said what it had always said — what she saw, what she feared, where she believed the girl was — and it stopped there. The wet hemline was a fact. The Harlow barn lie was a fact. The name Ambler beside the flower for war was a fact. And the old dock, the deep — that was not a fact. That was a suspicion. A teacher's thirty-two-year suspicion, aimed from the grave at the most beloved man in Blackwood Ridge, and it was not certainty.

Callie sat with it.

She sat with it the way she had learned to sit with difficult hands — not rushing past the discomfort, not naming it, just holding the glass steady and letting the thing be what it was. What it was: not enough. Not enough for a warrant, not enough for a search, not enough to walk into Cross's office and say *dig up the lake*. A dead woman's recorded seeing and a dead woman's suspicion and a wet hemline from 1994. The town had been dragged through a murder trial six months ago on stronger evidence than this. And the town — she could feel it without stepping outside, the way you feel weather in a bad knee — the town did not want to be dragged again.

She turned to the final plate.

A rose. *Rosa damascena* — the damask rose, hand-colored in a pink that had gone the color of old blood, and in the old language the rose meant *love*, and also it meant *secrecy*, and the Romans hung a rose above the council table to mean *what is said here stays here*. Marguerite had drawn a small precise cross beside the word *secrecy*, and beneath it, in the lightest pen pressure in the book — the hand of a woman running out of time — a single line.

*For the one who reads this. You know what I could not say. Say it.*

Callie closed the book.

She set the glass on the felt rest. She sat with her hands flat on the table and she breathed, and the breathing was uneven, and she did not try to make it even. A woman she had spoken to four times in her life had aimed her whole thirty-two-year silence at The Foxed Page, and now the asking was in Callie's hands, and the hands were shaking, and she let them shake.

The bell rang at the front.

She did not move. The bell rang again — not the customer's ring, but the knock-ring, the knuckle-on-glass that meant someone who knew the shop was closed and wanted in anyway. She stood. She went to the door.

It was Mae.

She was standing on the pavement in the last of the evening light with a dishcloth in her hands and her cardigan pulled close, and the lavender smell reached Callie before the face did — faint, strained, the sachet-and-cinnamon that was Mae's armor, thinner now but still there, still lavender, still Mae. She did not have soup. She was not carrying anything but the cloth and the look, and the not-carrying was its own sentence.

"Can I come in, honey."

Mae had used the word at the Dabney garden gate, two weeks ago, but it had been a wall — a welcome and a boundary in the same breath. This was not a wall. The word landed in Callie's chest like a thumb on a bruise. She held the door.

Mae came in and she did not go to the back room. She went to the reading nook by the front window, the one with the two leather chairs and the lamp with the green glass shade, and she sat, and she folded the cloth in her lap, and her hands worked the cloth. Callie sat across from her. The shop was dark except for the green lamp and the gold light leaking from the back room doorway.

"I need to tell you something," Mae said. "About Marguerite."

Callie waited.

Mae's hands worked the cloth. When she looked up, her eyes were wet.

"She came to see me," Mae said. "Last October. The cancer was in her bones by then — you could see it in the way she held the chair. She sat right where you're sitting. She asked me about you."

The shop was very quiet. Somewhere outside a dog was barking and a screen door slammed.

"She asked if you saw things through," Mae said. "She said she'd watched you for years — not at the auction, she said, at the counter, at the sales. She said you read what folks leave behind. The little marks." Mae's voice caught. "She said you don't skip over things. She said it the way a person says a thing they've been turning over for a long time." Mae's hands stopped on the cloth. "She asked if I thought you'd read a book all the way to the end. Even if the end was hard."

Callie's throat closed.

"I didn't say anything," Mae said. "I did what I do. I — I was careful. I told her you were busy. I changed the subject. I brought out the tea. I did the thing, Callie. The thing I always do." She looked down at the cloth. "She died before I understood what she'd been asking me."

"You understood," Callie said. Quietly. Not an accusation. A naming.

Mae's jaw worked. "I understood enough to be scared of it, honey. That ain't — that's not the same as knowing what to do."

She was quiet for a moment. The green lamp hummed. Mae's hands were still now — the first time Callie had seen them still in years — and the stillness was not peace. It was the stillness of a woman deciding, after decades of silence, to break her own habit.

"I should have told you in the garden," Mae said. "When Doris was there. I should have told you Marguerite meant the book for you. I knew. I knew when you said *estate lot*. I knew and I didn't say it because saying it would make it real." She stopped. Her eyes were wet and she did not wipe them. "I'm telling you now. That's what I've got. It's late. I know it's late."

Callie looked at her. Mae had done the thing Marguerite had done. She had been careful. And now she was choosing, late, to undo it.

"It's enough for tonight," Callie said. And then, because Mae's eyes were wet and she did not wipe them: "It's enough."

Mae nodded. She did not ask what Callie was going to do. She did not beg her to stop. She did not say *be careful*. She stood, and she folded the cloth one more time, and she touched Callie's shoulder — briefly, afraid of losing her — and she let herself out, and the bell rang behind her, and Callie was alone in the shop with the green lamp and the gold light from the back room and the book on the table and the knowing that Marguerite had chosen her, and Mae had confirmed it.

She sat in Mae's chair. It was still warm.

She could close the book and put it back on the shelf and let the silence hold, and the town would heal, and Doris would die in her kitchen with a bag of groceries she could not unpack, and the old dock at Blackwater Cove would keep what it kept, and Callie would be safe. She could be careful. That was the exit, and it was open, and she could see it.

She thought of Doris's hands flat on her thighs, the needles shaking, the voice that had said *find the rest of it before you come to my kitchen again.* Doris would learn it from the town, not from her, if she stopped now. That was the part she could not carry.

She made tea.

She stood at the counter in the dark shop and she made the bergamot the way Eleanor had taught her — the water off the boil, the cup warmed, the steep timed to the count Eleanor kept by tapping two fingers on the counter, one-two-three, one-two-three, the rhythm so deep in Callie's hands it would outlast memory. She drank it standing. It was almost right. It was closer to right than it had been in months — not Eleanor's register, not Eleanor's table, but a thing she had made herself, with her own hands, in a shop she had not lost. Almost right. Not yet.

She drank it and she let the deciding settle, and then she locked the book in the back room cabinet and she went upstairs, and she slept badly, and in the morning she went to the sheriff.

He was at his desk. The office smelled of coffee and floor cleaner and the staleness of a building where one man worked too many hours. He did not take off his hat when she came in. He always did — she had seen him do it a hundred times, the genuine respect of a man who'd been raised to — and today he did not. That was new. He looked up. He did not stand.

"Callie."

"I have something."

She set the book on his desk. She set her notes beside it — the decoded passages, the flower meanings, the timeline she had built, the map. She had copied it all in her own hand, neatly, on the archival paper she used for cataloguing, and she laid it out the way she would lay out a provenance file, with margins and dates and the annotations of a woman who knew the difference between evidence and suspicion and was showing him both.

Cross looked at it. He looked at it for a long time. He turned a page. He turned it back. He rubbed the back of his neck.

"This is handwriting," he said.

"It's a record. A witness record. She saw him come back from the lake the night Lauren vanished. Wet to the knees."

"She says he told the Carmody family he was at the Harlow barn," Cross said, reading.

"Yes. But when I went to see him — in his office — he told me he was at the party. He said they argued. He said he went home." Callie leaned forward. "That's two different stories, Sheriff. He told the Carmody family the Harlow barn. He told me the party and the house. And the cipher says he was at the lake."

Cross's jaw set. That was the tell — not the neck, the jaw. The one she had learned to read when a friend's name came into a room he didn't want it in.

"Thirty-two years ago."

"Yes."

"She's dead."

"Yes."

He set the pages down. He looked at her — the honest face of a man who liked Wells Ambler, who had leaned on him, who sat across from him at council meetings and considered him a friend, and who was being asked to treat him as a suspect in the death of a girl who had been gone for three decades.

"It's a book, Callie. It's a dead woman's notes in a book about flowers. I can't take that to a judge. I can't get a search warrant on *pen pressure*."

"I'm not asking for a warrant. I'm asking you to search the cove."

"Blackwater Cove." He said it flat. "You want me to drag Blackwater Cove. On the strength of — " he touched the page — "*water lily.*"

She held his gaze. She had expected this — the procedural wall, the evidence-in-a-baggie rigidity. What she had not expected was how long he had looked at the pages before he said no. In the winter, during the Ralston case, he would not have looked at all. He was dismissing her now, but he had read the whole thing first, and the reading was the thing that had not been there six months ago, and it was not partnership, but it was the shape of a door.

"The location is specific," she said. "The old dock. The deep. She wasn't guessing — she lived by the lake path. She knew the cove."

"She knew the cove," Cross repeated. "A woman who is dead. Knew a cove. Thirty-two years ago."

He rubbed his neck again. He looked at the pages one more time. Then he squared them on his desk — carefully — and he put his hat straight.

"I'll think about it," he said.

It was not *no*. It was not *yes*. It was the words of a man who had listened longer than he would have in the winter, and who was going to sit with it, and who might — or might not — do something about it, and the might-or-might-not was the most she was going to get, and she knew it, and she took it.

She left the book. She took her notes. She walked out into the late-spring morning, and the square was bright, and the peonies were open, and Harlan Beech was sweeping his pavement, and he looked up — he looked up, for the first time in weeks — and he did not speak, and she did not speak, but the looking-up was a thing, and she did not know what kind of thing, and she did not stop to find out.

She went back to the shop. She sat in the back room with the empty table where the book had been, and outside the mockingbird was running through every song it had ever stolen, and the town was going about its morning, and Callie Thorne had done the only thing she could do. She had said what a careful woman could not. And now the saying was in the sheriff's hands, and her hands were empty, and the empty was not peace and was not rest. It was the quiet of having decided.

Marguerite had written *say it*. Callie had said it. The rest was not hers.

***

## The Closing Ranks

It took three days for the town to decide what it thought of her, and the deciding was not kind.

Monday a mother named Linda Parrish came into the shop and asked, in the bright loud voice of a woman performing reasonableness, whether it was true that Callie was trying to reopen the Coalter case, and Callie said she was looking into Marguerite Dabney's annotations, and Linda Parrish said, "That's not what I heard," and left without buying anything, and the bell rang behind her and the sound was the sound of a door closing in a house that was not hers.

Tuesday the archive key was formalized. Harriet Vailes's gentle recall became a letter on council letterhead, hand-delivered by a clerk who would not meet her eye, stating that the archive system was under review and access would be restored "pending completion of the security audit," and the letter did not say when the audit would be complete. Wells Ambler had not come to her shop. He had not raised his voice. He had gone to the people who listened to him, which was most of them, and he had spoken with warmth, and the warmth had done what warmth does in a town that had just spent the winter bleeding — it had made everyone want the bleeding to stop, and Callie was the blade. She saw him once, through the shop window, shaking hands with Harlan Beech on the square. The palm was open. The grip was held a beat too long. She could read the effort in it now that she had not been able to read before, and the reading was its own kind of cost, because the man on the square was the same man who brought tomatoes to Doris Coalter, and the kindness was real, and the grave was real, and she could not make the two things fit together, and she did not try.

The garden club split.

The club met on Wednesdays in the basement of the old Historical Society building — closed as an institution since the Ralston money dried up, though the garden club had kept meeting because the lock on the side door had never been changed — and the meeting that week ran long and ran loud, and the sound of it carried through the open windows into the square. Half of the women remembered Lauren — her hands in the garden soil at the Dabney house, her laugh at the club meetings. Half of them revered Wells. And the halves did not agree on what Callie was doing, and the not-agreeing was a wound, because the garden club had been Marguerite's, and Marguerite had built it to hold the town together, and now it was pulling apart over the thing she had written down in flowers.

Doris pulled furthest.

She did not come to the shop. She did not come to the garden. She sent Mae, on Wednesday afternoon, with a message that was not unkind but was final, delivered in Mae's careful voice in the reading nook. The message was: Doris did not want to see Callie at the Dabney house again. Not until there was more than a margin note. Not until there was something Doris could hold.

"She's frightened," Mae said. "She's not angry, honey, she's frightened. The groceries — " Mae stopped. She did not finish the sentence. The groceries were the thing Doris could not afford to lose on the strength of a dead woman's shorthand, and Callie knew it, and Mae knew it, and neither of them said it, because saying it would have been saying that Doris loved the man she feared had killed her daughter, and the word *loved* was a thing neither of them could put in a room with the word *killed* and survive.

Mae stood to leave. At the door she paused, and her hand went to the latch, and she looked out toward the square — toward the sheriff's office — and Callie saw something in the set of her shoulders, a squaring, the posture of a woman who is not finished. Then Mae let herself out, and the bell rang behind her, and Callie did not know where she was going, and she did not ask.

By Thursday Callie had not had a customer in two days. Harlan Beech had swept his pavement each morning at the same hour, and on Thursday he slowed at her door — she saw him through the glass, hand on the frame, the broom in the other hand, and for a moment she thought he was going to come in. He did not. He straightened, and he swept past, and the not-coming-in was worse than the not-looking, because it meant he had decided.

She sat in the back room with the lamp on and the glass on the felt rest and the empty table where the book had been, and she was not decoding, because the book was at the sheriff's office and the decoding was done, and what she was doing was sitting, and the sitting had a weight she had not felt since the winter after Eleanor died — the particular gravity of a room that is both sanctuary and tomb. The room where her mother had died. The room that was hers now and had never stopped being Eleanor's. The room was quiet, and the quiet was not peace.

She had made tea and it had gone cold. The bergamot tasted almost right — still one register short of the thing she could not name, still not the taste she was looking for — and she set the cup down and she thought about stopping.

She could stop. She had done what Marguerite asked. She had said it. She had taken it to Cross. The saying was in his hands now, and his hands were procedural and slow and might do nothing with it. She reached for the one thing she had that was not suspicion — the Harlow barn, the party, two different stories told to two different audiences, a documented lie — and she held it up against the weight of the town and the weight of Doris's closed kitchen, and it was not enough. A lie was not a body. A wet hemline was not a confession.
